Chapter 6: The Power of Presence and the Subtle Art of Adaptation
There comes a moment in every journey when the old, familiar patterns just don’t cut it anymore. Imagine you’ve put in hours—maybe even years—honing your craft, whether it’s chess, martial arts, or something else you care about. And suddenly, you hit a wall. The strategies you relied on start falling short.
Picture yourself in a tense match. You’re focused, steady, and then... your opponent pulls off a move you never saw coming. It’s like they’ve tossed your entire playbook out the window. In that split second, you feel a jolt—a reminder that real mastery isn’t about sticking to a script. It’s about meeting the moment, right where you are.
That’s where presence comes in. If you’re not careful, your mind will start racing: “What if I lose?” “Why didn’t I see that coming?” Or maybe it’s stuck on old mistakes. But here’s the thing—when you manage to anchor your attention right here, right now, that’s when the magic happens.
There’s a story I love about a competitor who kept losing, over and over. Every time they sat down at the board, their mind was packed with worries—about their reputation, what others expected, or the sting of past defeats. But everything changed the moment they let all that go. When they finally focused on the board in front of them, the person across the table, and the possibilities in each move, their game started to flow again. It was like they’d rediscovered what made them love the game in the first place.
The same lesson shows up in the dojo. During a sparring session, your opponent shifts—maybe it’s a subtle change in their stance, or a move you haven’t seen before. There’s no time to stop and analyze, no chance to retreat into theory. You just have to respond—feel, adapt, and trust all those hours of practice to guide you. In those moments, it’s crystal clear: adaptability isn’t just a skill, it’s a mindset. It’s about meeting each new moment with openness, not fear.
Most of us don’t realize how often we resist change—clinging to what worked yesterday, hoping it’ll work again today. But real growth? It comes from letting go, stepping into the unknown, and believing that what you’ve learned will carry you through. When your mind is calm and alert, creativity has room to breathe. Suddenly, what felt like a setback becomes an invitation to experiment, to find new solutions.
And this isn’t just about competition. When you take this way of being into everyday life—your conversations, your work, even your toughest conflicts—something shifts. Instead of trying to control everything, you start listening, really listening. You show up fully. And you find that doors open—not because you forced them, but because you were truly present.
In the end, the art of learning is the art of showing up—again and again—ready to meet whatever comes your way. That’s where true transformation begins.
